question: A family in rural Bihar sells land to pay for hospitalisation of their father with a stroke, spending 40% of their annual household income on healthcare. Which health economics concept BEST describes this situation?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Catastrophic health expenditure is defined as out-of-pocket health spending exceeding a threshold of household income — commonly 10% of total household income or 40% of non-food (capacity-to-pay) income. This family's 40% expenditure clearly meets this threshold.

Impoverishing expenditure specifically refers to spending that pushes a household below the poverty line. While this family may be impoverished, the defining concept for spending exceeding a percentage of income threshold is 'catastrophic' health expenditure.

Social health insurance involves pre-paid, pooled contributions (like ESI or CGHS). Out-of-pocket payment at the point of care — especially distress asset sales — is the opposite of insurance-based financing.
Government health expenditure is funded from public revenues. This scenario describes a family paying directly from their own resources (out-of-pocket), not government spending.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key phrase is '40% of annual household income.' When out-of-pocket spending exceeds a threshold proportion of income, it is classified as 'catastrophic health expenditure' — not impoverishing (which specifically crosses the poverty line) and not insurance-based.

Well done. Catastrophic health expenditure is the correct term when OOP spending exceeds a defined share of household income or capacity to pay. India's high OOP share (~60% of total health expenditure) makes this a common scenario — and the core justification for PM-JAY/Ayushman Bharat.
